summary: Wayne Hathaway backs Edwin Meyer's opposition in RFC 492 to the fixes proposed in RFC 467, arguing that they hide the real problem of lost messages. He proposes using an unused byte in the message leader as a Sequence Control Byte, a count that lets the receiving NCP spot a lost message.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 512 proposes adding a Sequence Control Byte (SCB) to host messages so a receiving NCP can detect a missing message. A zero SCB disables checking, allowing existing NCPs to continue using zero in the unused field.

questions: how to detect lost messages in ncp
subtitle: A proposal to detect lost host messages with a Sequence Control Byte in each message.

tldr.problem: The author argues that allocation-reset fixes can conceal a more general problem: messages may be lost between hosts.
tldr.mechanism: A receiving NCP checks a per-link Sequence Control Byte against the expected count and can report a mismatch with an ERR message.
tldr.outcome: The proposal uses zero to mean no checking, so existing NCPs need not change unless they choose to use the check. It is presented as an interim approach.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 512's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The memo presents the SCB as an interim proposal for the host-to-host protocol.

sections.title: Detect Lost Messages Directly
sections.content: Wayne Hathaway agrees with Meyer's opposition in RFC 492 to the proposed fixes in RFC 467 for the lost allocate and half-closed phenomena. He also agrees that resetting allocations can hide the underlying problem of lost messages. RFC 512 proposes a way to recognize those losses.
sections.plainLanguage: The author argues that resetting allocation counters may hide lost messages. The proposal aims to make a missing message visible when it reaches the receiver.

sections.title: The Sequence Control Byte
sections.content:
The proposal designates one of the two unused 8-bit bytes in the Level 2 message leader as a Sequence Control Byte (SCB). It acts as a modulo 255 message count for each link. When a message arrives, the receiving NCP compares the SCB with the value expected from the previous message on that link.

A mismatch indicates that a message was lost. The receiving NCP could report the received and expected values in an ERR message, which the memo says still needed definition. The message with an unexpected SCB should still be processed, and the next expected value is computed from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a count for its link. If the next count is not what the receiver expects, the receiver can report a possible loss.

sections.title: Compatibility with Existing NCPs
sections.content:
An SCB of zero means no checking is performed. The value after 255 is 1. Because the Level 2 protocol specifies that the two bytes are zero, existing NCPs would not need to change unless they wanted to use checking. RST and ERR messages could also use zero to bypass checking and avoid loops.

The author compares this proposal with the per-host message numbering in RFC 516. RFC 512's count is per link, so it does not require all messages between a pair of hosts to arrive in the order sent. Hathaway calls it an interim solution because host-to-host acknowledgments would require larger Level 2 protocol changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Zero keeps checking off, so older NCPs can leave the field unchanged. The proposed count is per link, rather than one count shared by all traffic between two hosts.

references.text: RFC 467, the proposals on lost allocate and half-closed phenomena discussed in this memo.
Meyer, E., RFC 492, response to RFC 467.
Postel, J., "Lost Message Detection", RFC 516, May 1973.
